title: Teaching Success in a Noisy World
author: Stuart Jr., Dave
summary: Stuart argues that the defining problem facing both teachers and students is not information but noise, meaning the sheer volume of choices that modern life presents. He builds the case from Peter Drucker by way of Greg McKeown's Essentialism, taking the designer Dieter Rams's maxim of less but better as a working principle for classrooms and for teaching lives. The move the piece makes is to treat noise reduction as teachable content rather than a private discipline. He contrasts two students, one with a crowded apartment and an unrestricted phone and one with her own room and an enforced study hour, to show that self-management is unequally distributed and therefore has to be taught rather than demanded. He borrows Angela Duckworth's idea that students should become the teachers of their own bedroom classrooms, and recommends a five to ten minute warm-up activity rather than a new unit. The final third turns the argument back on the teacher, cataloguing the author's own restrictions on phone apps, email notifications, television and video games. The closing claim is that teaching noise reduction is only credible when the teacher practises it.
points: Stuart reframes information overload as a choice problem, following Drucker's claim that managing oneself is the genuinely new human condition and therefore the skill schools have no tested model for teaching.

The Naddyia and Paris contrast is the article's sharpest instructional point: exhortations to be grittier are useless when a student's home environment supplies the obstacle, so environment design has to be taught explicitly.
He caps the intervention deliberately at a five to ten minute whole-class writing and discussion activity so that self-management instruction never displaces content and curriculum.

The author distinguishes resisting noise from eliminating it and argues that elimination is the lazy and therefore durable strategy, citing his own removal of the browser and email notifications from his phone.
The piece ties teacher credibility to teacher practice, arguing that being a saner teacher means living the noise reduction you assign to students.
quotes: I've written before on information overload , but a recent read gave me a much better word for what I'm getting at: noise . You and I and every one of our students live in a world so unprecedentedly full of noise that we, as a species, are literally figuring out how to deal with it for the first time.

This is clarifying. The problem isn't just information — it's the choices so much information presents us with. How, then, do we teach our students (and ourselves) to manage themselves when we have next to no historically validated model for doing so?
If we're going to manage ourselves better — and help our students do the same — noise reduction is the place to start. This is, according to Drucker, perhaps the 21st century skill.

But noise reduction is way harder for some of our kids than it is for others. Ninth grader Naddyia, who shares a one bedroom apartment with five family members and has unlimited use of her smart phone, has a lot more work to do than her classmate Paris, who has her own bedroom and a mandatory “no cell phone” study time each night. You can't just tell Naddyia to “be grittier” or “do her homework” if you're going to do all in your power to promote her long-term flourishing .

When I talk to my kids about Duckworth's bedroom classroom concept, I don't expect that it will lead to drastic life changes for all of them. I do expect, though, that of my 100+ students, a percentage are going to take the idea and run. And, since I don't invest a ton of time into this — again, we're talking a 5-10 minute warm-up style activity that won't sideline my content and curricula — I'd call this a fantastic use of time.
Rather, it's that being a better and saner teacher means practicing what we teach . If we're going to teach noise reduction, we need to practice it ourselves.
